description: Hand-authored semantic search evaluation corpus for asymmetric (E5-style) embedding models. Queries use the implicit 'query: ' role, documents the implicit 'document: ' role. Content is developer-tools prose (Rust, concurrency, git, testing, observability, containers, databases, networking, security, embeddings/ML, CI/CD, code review, issue tracking, config management) reflecting what kaijutsu and kaibo actually search over, plus a small Japanese slice to exercise multilingual retrieval.

documents.text: In Rust, each value has a single owner, and when that owner goes out of scope the value is dropped automatically.
Moving a value in Rust transfers ownership to the new binding, so the original variable can no longer be used unless the type implements Copy.
The borrow checker enforces that you can have either one mutable reference or many immutable references to a value, but never both at the same time.
Lifetimes in Rust are annotations that tell the compiler how long references are valid relative to each other, without changing runtime behavior.
A common beginner error is trying to return a reference to a local variable, which fails because the local's lifetime ends when the function returns.
Rc<T> allows multiple owners of the same heap-allocated value by tracking a reference count, but it only works within a single thread.
The Clone trait creates a deep copy of a value, which is useful when you need two independent owners instead of fighting the borrow checker.
std::sync::Mutex wraps a value and only allows access to it through a MutexGuard obtained by calling lock, which blocks until the mutex is free.
Unlike a Mutex, an RwLock allows many simultaneous readers or a single writer, which helps read-heavy workloads avoid contention.
Rust's async/await syntax compiles futures into state machines, but you still need an executor like tokio to actually poll and run them.
Channels in std::sync::mpsc let one or more producer threads send values to a single consumer thread without shared mutable state.
A deadlock occurs when two threads each hold a lock the other is waiting for; Rust's type system does not prevent this at compile time.
Arc<Mutex<T>> is the idiomatic way to share mutable state across threads in Rust: Arc handles shared ownership, Mutex handles exclusive access.
Poisoning happens when a thread panics while holding a Mutex lock; subsequent lock() calls return an Err to signal the guarded data may be inconsistent.
The Result<T, E> type forces callers to handle both the success and failure cases explicitly instead of relying on exceptions.
The question mark operator propagates an Err up to the caller automatically, which is why most Rust functions that can fail return a Result.
anyhow::Error is a good fit for application code where you just want to bubble up any error with context, while thiserror suits libraries that need typed errors.
panic! unwinds the stack (or aborts the process, depending on the panic strategy), and should be reserved for unrecoverable bugs, not expected failures.
Option<T> represents the presence or absence of a value, and unwrap() on a None will panic, so map_or or match are usually safer in production code.
Wrapping a low-level I/O error with .context("failed to read config file") preserves the original error while adding information about what the caller was trying to do.
git rebase rewrites commit history by replaying your commits on top of another branch, producing a linear history but changing commit hashes.
git merge combines two branches by creating a new merge commit that has two parents, preserving the original history exactly as it happened.
Force-pushing after a rebase is necessary because the rewritten commits have different hashes than what's on the remote, but it can destroy teammates' work if they've already pulled.
git bisect performs a binary search through commit history to find the exact commit that introduced a regression, given a known-good and known-bad commit.
A git worktree lets you check out a second branch into its own directory without cloning the repo again, useful for working on a PR while keeping main untouched.
Squashing commits with an interactive rebase collapses several small commits into one, which keeps the history readable at the cost of losing intermediate steps.
Test-driven development means writing a failing test before writing the code that makes it pass, which forces you to define the interface before the implementation.
A flaky test passes and fails intermittently without code changes, usually because of timing assumptions, shared state, or network calls that should be mocked.
Property-based testing generates many random inputs and checks that an invariant holds for all of them, catching edge cases example-based tests miss.
Fixture files capture real-world inputs, like an actual API response or config file, so tests exercise realistic data instead of hand-crafted stubs.
Golden file tests compare a program's output against a checked-in reference file, failing loudly whenever the output changes unexpectedly.
Mocking a dependency replaces it with a fake implementation during a test, trading realism for speed and determinism.
OpenTelemetry defines a vendor-neutral format for traces, metrics, and logs, so instrumentation code doesn't need to change when you switch backends.
A trace is a tree of spans representing the path a single request took through a distributed system, including timing for each hop.
Structured logging emits log lines as key-value pairs or JSON instead of free text, making them easy to query and correlate with traces.
The OTLP protocol is how OpenTelemetry SDKs export telemetry data to a collector, typically over gRPC or HTTP with protobuf payloads.
High-cardinality labels on metrics, like a raw user ID, can blow up the storage cost of a time-series database because each unique combination becomes its own series.
Sampling traces at the collector, rather than at every service, keeps overhead low while still capturing a representative slice of traffic.
A span's parent-child relationship reconstructs causality across service boundaries, which is what makes distributed tracing different from per-service logging.
A multi-stage Dockerfile builds the binary in a heavier image with the full toolchain, then copies just the artifact into a minimal runtime image based on distroless.
A multi-stage Dockerfile builds the binary in a heavier image with the full toolchain, then copies just the artifact into a minimal alpine-based runtime image.
Kubernetes liveness probes restart a container that stops responding, while readiness probes control whether traffic is routed to it at all.
A rolling deployment replaces old pods with new ones gradually, keeping some capacity of each version available during the transition to avoid downtime.
Setting resource requests and limits on a pod tells the scheduler how much CPU and memory to reserve, and caps how much the container can consume.
A sidecar container runs alongside the main application container in the same pod, commonly used for log shipping or a service mesh proxy.
Row-level locking in a relational database prevents two transactions from modifying the same row concurrently, but can cause one transaction to block waiting for another.
An index speeds up lookups on a column at the cost of extra storage and slower writes, since every insert or update must also update the index.
A database migration is a versioned, ordered script that changes the schema, letting a team apply the same changes consistently across environments.
Optimistic locking checks a version column before committing a write and rejects it if another transaction changed the row first, avoiding long-held locks.
A deadlock in a database occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other transaction needs, and the database detects and aborts one of them.
Connection pooling reuses a fixed number of open database connections across requests instead of opening a new TCP connection for every query.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE explicitly locks the selected rows until the current transaction commits or rolls back, preventing other transactions from modifying them.
TCP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery of a byte stream by retransmitting lost packets and acknowledging received ones, at the cost of higher latency than UDP.
TLS establishes an encrypted channel over an existing TCP connection through a handshake that negotiates a cipher suite and verifies the server's certificate.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over a single TCP connection, avoiding the head-of-line blocking that plagued HTTP/1.1's connection-per-request model.
A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers, terminating TLS and routing requests based on path or host, and is often where rate limiting lives.
DNS resolution translates a hostname into an IP address by querying a chain of nameservers, and results are cached according to a record's TTL.
gRPC uses HTTP/2 as its transport and protobuf for serialization, giving it lower overhead than JSON-over-HTTP for service-to-service calls.
A PII detector scans text for sensitive spans like email addresses, credit card numbers, and API keys, typically using a BIOES tagging scheme over token sequences.
Secrets like API keys and private keys should never be committed to version control; a pre-commit hook that scans staged diffs catches most accidental leaks.
OAuth2's authorization code flow exchanges a short-lived code for an access token, keeping the token itself out of the browser's URL and history.
A JWT is a signed token containing claims that a server can verify without a database lookup, but revoking one before it expires requires an extra mechanism like a blocklist.
Rate limiting an authentication endpoint slows down credential-stuffing attacks by capping how many login attempts a client can make in a time window.
A connection string that embeds a database password in plaintext is a common secret that leaks through logs, environment dumps, or crash reports.
Principle of least privilege means a service account should only have the permissions it needs for its specific task, not broad admin access.
An embedding model maps text into a fixed-size vector such that semantically similar text ends up close together under cosine similarity.
Asymmetric embedding models like E5 use different prefixes for queries and documents, such as 'query: ' and 'document: ', because the two roles aren't interchangeable.
Tokenization splits raw text into subword units before a model can process it; a byte-pair encoding tokenizer builds its vocabulary from the most frequent merges in a training corpus.
Approximate nearest neighbor search trades a small amount of recall for a large speedup over exact search when querying millions of embedding vectors.
A bidirectional encoder attends to the entire input sequence in both directions, unlike a causal decoder that can only attend to earlier tokens.
Hard negatives are examples that are superficially similar to a query but actually irrelevant, and including them in training or evaluation makes a retrieval system much harder to fool.
Truncating an embedding model's input at a fixed token limit, like 512 tokens, means very long documents get silently cut off unless they're chunked first.
Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors regardless of their magnitude, which is why embeddings are often normalized to unit length before comparison.
A CI pipeline runs the test suite automatically on every push, catching regressions before they reach a reviewer instead of relying on manual testing.
Caching dependencies between CI runs, like a cargo target directory, cuts build times significantly but risks stale artifacts if the cache key doesn't account for lockfile changes.
A matrix build runs the same job across multiple combinations of OS and language version in parallel to catch platform-specific failures early.
Continuous deployment automatically ships every change that passes CI to production, which requires a high level of trust in the test suite's coverage.
A pre-commit hook runs fast checks like formatting and linting locally before a commit is even created, catching issues before they hit CI.
Branch protection rules require a pull request to pass CI and get at least one approval before it can be merged into main.
A good code review comment explains why a change is a problem, not just that it is, so the author can learn instead of just fixing the one instance.
Reviewing a large PR in one sitting tends to miss more bugs than reviewing several smaller PRs, because attention degrades with diff size.
Nitpick comments about style should be clearly labeled as optional so the author doesn't waste time debating something that doesn't block the merge.
Requesting changes on a PR blocks it from merging until the author addresses the feedback or the reviewer approves a follow-up commit.
Reviewing without a diff, and instead reading the whole file in context, catches design issues that a line-by-line diff view tends to hide.
A second opinion from a different reviewer, especially one who wasn't involved in the design discussion, tends to catch different classes of problems.
A well-written bug report includes steps to reproduce, the expected behavior, and the actual behavior, so a reviewer doesn't have to guess at context.
Labeling an issue 'good first issue' signals it's scoped small enough for a new contributor to tackle without deep familiarity with the codebase.
Linking a pull request to the issue it closes lets the tracker automatically close the issue when the PR merges.
A stale-bot automatically comments on and eventually closes issues that haven't seen activity in a set number of days, to keep the backlog manageable.
Triage means deciding an issue's priority and whether it belongs on the current milestone, not necessarily who will fix it.
A regression is a bug where something that used to work stops working after a change, which is why bisecting against an older release is often the fastest way to find the cause.
A config file's schema should be validated at startup so a typo in a key name fails loudly immediately, instead of silently falling back to a default deep in the code.
Environment variables are a common way to inject configuration into a container without baking secrets into the image itself.
A feature flag lets a change be deployed to production while disabled, then enabled gradually for a subset of users without a new deploy.
Layering configuration, where a base file is overridden by an environment-specific file, which is in turn overridden by environment variables, gives predictable precedence.
A silent fallback to a default value when a required config key is missing can mask a deployment mistake for a long time before anyone notices.
Storing default values directly in the schema, rather than scattered through the code, makes it obvious what a config field will do if left unset.
Rustの所有権システムでは、各値には所有者が一人だけ存在し、所有者がスコープを抜けると値は自動的に破棄される。
Mutexはロックを取得したスレッドだけがデータへアクセスできることを保証するが、パニックが起きるとロックが「毒される」ことがある。
git rebaseはコミット履歴を書き換えて別のブランチの上にコミットを再適用するため、共有ブランチで使うとチームメイトの作業を壊す危険がある。
分散トレーシングでは、一つのリクエストがマイクロサービス群をどう通過したかをスパンの木構造として記録する。
PII検出器はメールアドレスやAPIキーなど機密情報をテキストから検出するが、コネクション文字列に埋め込まれたパスワードも検出対象になる。
非対称な埋め込みモデルでは、クエリには「query: 」、文書には「document: 」という異なるプレフィックスを付与する必要がある。
A connection pool caps the number of concurrent database connections a service opens, reusing idle connections instead of establishing a new one for every query.
Moving a value in Rust transfers ownership outright; unlike C++, there's no implicit copy constructor invoked unless the type explicitly derives Copy or Clone.
